extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, privacy advocates, policy counsel, and attorneys who participate in or challenge agency rulemakings, adjudications, licensing, or judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the Administrative Procedure Act's requirements and standards governing agency rulemaking, adjudication, licensing, and judicial review, intended to help public commenters, advocates, and counsel understand procedural and substantive criteria for agency actions and challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a "rule"
rubrics_metrics.description: "The whole or a part of an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy or describing the organization, procedure, or practice requirements of an agency..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In short, an agency creates a rule when it seeks to "implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy." The quoted statutory definition continues to include future prescriptions (rates, wages, corporate or financial structures, prices, facilities, services, valuations, costs, accounting, or practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements for proposed rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency typically must give a notice of a proposed rulemaking published in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice must include the date the rule will come into effect, the legal authority the agency proposes to act under, and the substance of the rule. The Federal Register is "the official daily publication for rules, proposed rules, and notices of Federal agencies..."

rubrics_metrics.name: Public comment solicitation and consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: After notice is given, the agency is required to solicit and accept public comments on the rule and must consider all of the comments that are submitted in passing the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no minimum comment-period length specified by the APA; most comment periods last between 30 and 60 days and may be re-opened if the agency believes more time or more feedback is necessary. Agencies must actually consider submitted comments when issuing the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal rulemaking triggers (when formal hearing 'on the record' is required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal rulemaking, which requires a courtroom-style hearing with evidence given and received on the record, is appropriate where a statute provides rules are "required to be made on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing" or in rulemakings involving adjudicative facts or facts specific to the rights of an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a statute requires more than informal notice-and-comment but less than full formal rulemaking, a hybrid rulemaking may blend elements of both procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to notice-and-comment rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA describes both general and specific exceptions where notice-and-comment is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General exceptions: (1) the Rule involves a military or foreign affairs function of the United States; (2) the Rule involves a matter relating to agency management or personnel or to public property, loans, grants, benefits, or contracts. Specific exceptions: (1) interpretative rules, general statements of policy, or rules of agency organization, procedure, or practice; (2) when the agency finds for "good cause" that notice-and-comment is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. Courts apply a functional analysis to determine if a rule is procedural or substantive (see Air Transp. Ass'n v. Dep't of Transp.). Under the good-cause exception, an agency's own delay cannot create good cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal vs informal adjudications and required procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudications may be formal or informal; formal adjudication is required when statute calls for action "on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing," and formal adjudications require evidence introduced on the record and an Administrative Law Judge to preside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The APA does not set procedures for informal adjudications (left to agencies). In formal adjudication, notice must be given to the individual (time, place, nature of hearing, legal authority and jurisdiction, and matters of asserted fact and law). Agencies may initiate actions without a private plaintiff, but private parties with standing to appeal may intervene. Final agency decisions in adjudications can be held final or appealed to the full agency and are subject to judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process requirements for adjudications
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjudications are subject to due process protections when (1) the hearing involves adjudicative facts (affecting a small, individualized group) and (2) there is possibility of deprivation of a property or liberty interest created and defined by existing rules or independent sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is derived from Board of Regents v. Roth and limits when formal due process procedures must be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice requirements for formal adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency must give notice to an individual subject to a formal adjudication that includes the time, place, and nature of the hearing, the legal authority and jurisdiction, and the matters of asserted fact and law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide required notice can affect the legality of the proceeding; parties with standing to appeal generally may intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing procedural standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When a license is required by law, the agency in granting that license must comply with the same procedures governing formal rulemaking and adjudication; other licenses are governed by internal agency rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency cannot revoke a license while an application for a new license remains pending. Licenses cannot be revoked unless the agency gives notice specifying what action provided cause for revocation and allows the licensee an opportunity to correct the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review availability and statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Final agency decisions are subject to judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges to agency regulations generally have a six-year statute of limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: The reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of law, interpret constitutional and statutory provisions, and determine the meaning or applicability of the terms of an agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court must (A) compel agency action unlawfully withheld or unreasonably delayed and (B) set aside agency action, findings, and conclusions that meet specified unlawful criteria (see next metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for setting aside agency action (APA §706-type grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reviewing court may find agency action unlawful and set it aside if it is: (1) arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with law; (2) contrary to constitutional right, power, privilege, or immunity; (3) in excess of statutory jurisdiction, authority, or limitations, or short of statutory right; (4) without observance of procedure required by law; (5) unsupported by substantial evidence in cases subject to 5 U.S.C. §§ 556–557 or otherwise reviewed on the record; or (6) unwarranted by the facts to the extent facts are subject to trial de novo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the classic grounds under which courts may vacate or remand agency actions; each ground has distinct legal standards and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of review: substantial evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'substantial evidence' standard is required for formal rulemaking and formal adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts uphold agency decisions if the decision is reasonable or the record contains such evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion. Actions invalidated under this standard are typically abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of review: arbitrary and capricious (reasoned decisionmaking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'arbitrary and capricious' standard is mainly applied to informal rulemakings and informal adjudications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether the decision was based on consideration of relevant factors and whether there was a clear error of judgment (Citizens to Preserve Overton Park v. Volpe). Courts may not probe why particular data were relied upon but may inquire what data the agency reviewed. Under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, the agency must examine relevant data and "articulate a satisfactory explanation" including a "rational connection between facts and judgment." When action is invalidated under this standard, courts typically remand to the agency to supplement the record or justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of review: statutory interpretation (Chevron two-step)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'statutory interpretation' standard involves a two-step analysis from Chevron U.S.A., Inc. v. NRDC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: Determine whether Congress has spoken to the precise question at issue (look to statute language, design, and canons). Step 2: If Congress has not directly addressed the precise issue, determine whether the agency's action is a permissible construction of the statute. Under Chevron, legislative regulations are given deference unless arbitrary, capricious, or manifestly contrary to the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed judicial review (law and fact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed judicial review encompasses review of both law and fact underlying agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review of law examines statutory authority for the regulation; review of fact examines the agency's factual findings that guided its decision-making. Different standards (deference/independence) can apply to each component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to obtain judicial review (four elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who suffer a 'legal wrong because of agency action' or are 'adversely affected or aggrieved by agency action within the meaning of a relevant statute' have standing; four elements must be proven: (1) injury in fact; (2) causation; (3) redressability; and (4) zone of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Injury in fact: agency action affecting environmental, aesthetic, or recreational interests can qualify (Sierra Club v. Morton); must directly affect personal interests rather than merely corporate interests, and third-party injuries can suffice if direct. Causation: a connection between the injury and the agency action. Redressability: likelihood that judicial relief will remedy the injury. Zone of interest: the injury must be the type protected by the statute or regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency duty to publish in the Federal Register and identify authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must publish notices, rules, and related actions in the Federal Register and identify the legal authority under which they act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication ensures public notice and provides the basis for comment and for later judicial review of whether the agency acted within its authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on invoking 'good cause' to avoid notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may omit notice-and-comment if it finds "good cause" that the process is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts scrutinize good-cause claims; agencies cannot manufacture good cause by delaying action themselves. Functional analysis and precedent inform when good cause is appropriate.
